title: Like milk and water
hookLine: Buddhists of different schools meet in shared councils, such as the World Fellowship of Buddhists
carry: samaggi: different in body, one in mind

cards: The monks at Kosambi are fighting. In the Pali account, they've split into sides over a point of discipline, and the quarrel has turned to sharp words. The Buddha asks them to stop.
They tell him, more or less, to leave it to them. So he does. He walks off alone.
On the way, he comes to a small park where three monks are living together, and stops to ask them a question.

teach.b: The three are Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila. The Buddha asks how they are getting on, and Anuruddha says they live together blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kindly eyes. How?
Each one, he says, sets aside what he himself wants and does what the others want. We are different in body, he says, but one in mind. Then he gets practical.
Whoever comes back first from the alms round sets out the seats and the water. Whoever comes back last eats what's left and cleans up.
Whoever sees the water pot empty fills it, and if it's too heavy, he waves another over, and they lift it together without a word.
Seats, water, a heavy pot. Not agreement on every point. Kindness in the chores.

Buddhists from different lands and schools, Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana, meet in shared bodies such as the World Fellowship of Buddhists. Meeting doesn't merge their schools or settle every question.
They sit in one room, share a meal, and learn each other's customs, the robes and festivals and languages of this week.
Behind it is a line from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love."
Kosambi is the warning. The three in the park are the model.

how: Buddhists of different schools meet in shared bodies such as the World Fellowship of Buddhists, and in local councils and joint celebrations, where they share meals and learn each other's customs while keeping their own traditions.

o: all the schools joining into one new Buddhist church
schools coming together side by side, without merging
a yearly debate to settle which school is correct

games.q: like milk and water: tap the pairs.

s: the three monks in the park agreed on every point
their secret was kindness in the chores: seats, water, a pot lifted together.
Anuruddha says they are different in body but one in mind
he tells the Buddha they live blending like milk and water.
shared councils ask the schools to merge into one
they meet and learn each other's customs while keeping their own traditions.

games.q: you're one of three monks sharing a small park. the water pot is empty and too heavy to lift alone. what do you do?
o: leave it for whoever comes next.
wave another monk over and lift it together.
call a meeting about whose turn it is.
games.why: in Anuruddha's telling, they wave someone over and lift it together without breaking the silence.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose way is different from yours: another school, another faith, another habit of doing the same good thing.
If it feels natural, bring your palms together at your chest, a greeting used in Buddhist lands, and bow your head a little toward them.
Then think of one heavy pot you might lift together, and wish them well, in your own words or none.

wordCard.voice: Meeting each other. Buddhists of different schools coming together, not to merge, but to live and work side by side, like milk and water. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samaggi: concord, a community living in harmony.

carryVoice: Your line: samaggi, different in body, one in mind. One water pot, lifted together. Rest well.
